I am 74 years old and have farmed my six mu of land in Quzhou County my whole life. My body is not as strong as it used to be, but I still know every inch of this soil. Around here, everyone follows the wheat-maize rotation — it is the only way to make a living from the land. My winter wheat went into the ground last October, as it always does, and now that spring has arrived I need to irrigate it and top-dress it with fertilizer. I do not chase newfangled ideas; I plant what my neighbors plant and what the seed shop in town recommends. For wheat, I use Luyuan502 or Zhongxinmai99 — they are reliable and give me about 1,000 jin per mu. For summer maize, I will sow Denghai605 right after the wheat harvest in early June; it is a hybrid seed that has given good yields for years, around 1,000 jin per mu or a bit more. 

I do the wheat planting with rotary tillage to prepare a fine seedbed, but there is no time to till for maize — we plant it no-tillage straight into the wheat stubble, sometimes with a little straw return. I will irrigate the wheat three or four times: the winter irrigation, one at jointing, one at heading, and maybe one more if the weather turns dry. The maize only needs one or two irrigations, usually if the summer drought hits. For fertilizer, I spread compound fertilizer as a basal dose and then top-dress with urea. The wheat needs more nitrogen — roughly 55 kg per mu — while the maize needs less, around 20 kg per mu. I spray pesticides about three or four times for the wheat and about three times for the maize, mostly insecticides and herbicides. My son helps me with the heavy labor and machine work when he is not working in town. At my age, I keep things simple and stick to what works.

I prepare the seedbed for wheat with rotary tillage, but maize is planted no-tillage right after wheat harvest because there is no time to plough. I fertilize wheat more heavily, especially with nitrogen, and irrigate it four times, while maize needs less water and fewer nutrients.
